title: Peltier (thermoelectric) cooler box
summary: Fit a salvaged Peltier module between two heatsinks in the wall of an insulated box to make a 12V cooler. It cools 10–20 °C below the air around it and draws 40–70W, so it is power-hungry: good for drinks, small amounts of food and medicine on a big battery or solar, not a full fridge.

materials.item: Heatsinks: a large hot-side one with a fan (a desktop CPU cooler is ideal) and a smaller cold-side one
12V fans: one for the hot side, a small one inside
Insulated box or picnic cooler, food-safe inside (or keep food in sealed containers)
Extra insulation for walls and lid
Aluminium spacer block, if the wall is thicker than the module
Fuse and holder, 7.5–10A per module, within 30 cm of battery +
Buck converter to run the module at 7–9V for better efficiency
12V battery or 12V power supply of 6A or more
Long screws with insulating washers, foam to seal gaps

steps.text: Find the cold side: put the module on the hot-side heatsink with a little paste, connect red to + and black to − on 12V for 2–3 seconds, and touch the top face. If it's cold, that face goes inside the box.
steps.warn: Without a heatsink the module overheats and burns out within seconds, and its hot face can burn you. Only test briefly.

steps.text: Cut a hole in the box wall or lid just big enough for the module (or the spacer block if the wall is thick). Mount it high in the box: cold air sinks.
Build the sandwich: hot-side heatsink outside, module, spacer block if needed, cold-side heatsink inside. Spread a thin, even layer of paste on every contact face.
Clamp with screws through both heatsinks, tightening a little at a time in a cross pattern. Use plastic or fibre washers so the screws don't carry heat back in.
steps.warn: Over-tightening or uneven clamping cracks the ceramic module.

steps.text: Seal every gap round the sandwich with foam. Any air leak wastes most of the cooling.
Fit the hot-side fan to blow onto the outside fins, and a small fan inside to stir air over the cold sink.
Wire the module and both fans in parallel to the 12V supply through a switch and the fuse. Put the fuse within 30 cm of battery positive.
steps.warn: Fuse at the battery. A shorted 14 AWG wire from a battery gets hot enough to burn.

steps.text: Optional: wire a thermostat to switch the module (through a relay if its contacts are small) and set it to 4–8 °C.
Run it empty for 1–2 hours and measure the inside temperature. Touch the hot-side heatsink: it should stay below about 50 °C. If it's hotter, use a bigger heatsink or fan.
steps.warn: If the hot-side fan stops, the module overheats and can fail within a minute. Check the fan whenever you open the box.

steps.text: Use it well: put in only food that's already cool, open it rarely, keep it in shade, and add frozen water bottles when you have them. Drain condensation regularly.

notes:
## What to expect
- A 12V 6A module draws about 50–70W and moves at most about 50W of heat, less as the temperature difference grows. Its efficiency (heat moved per watt in) is about 0.3–0.6. A compressor fridge is 3–5× better.
- In a good picnic cooler it holds about 10–20 °C below room temperature. At 30 °C outside that's 10–20 °C inside, not 4 °C.
- Two modules side by side cool faster but use double the power.

## Power budget
60W × 24 h = 1,440Wh a day, more than a 100Ah lead-acid battery can give. Run it on a thermostat and the duty falls to 30–60% in a well-insulated box. Solar: roughly 250–500W of panel to run one module, depending on duty and sun.

## Run it at lower voltage
At 7–9V a 12V module moves less heat but uses far less power, so it's more efficient (often 1.5–2× better). With a buck converter, run it at reduced voltage all the time once the box is cold.

## Insulation does half the job
Heat leaking in = area × temperature difference ÷ insulation. Doubling wall thickness halves the leak. Add foam board or blankets around the outside of a thin cooler, and seal the lid.

## Medicine
Many medicines need 2–8 °C. A Peltier box may not reach that on hot days. Check with a thermometer before trusting it, and keep a cool-water or clay-pot evaporative backup.

## Variations
- Swap polarity and it becomes a warmer (useful for keeping food warm or for an egg incubator; set a thermostat).
- Thermoelectric generators: a module between a stove and a cold sink gives a few watts. Use generator-rated modules where possible; cooling modules can be damaged by stove heat over about 130–150 °C.

## Where to find modules
Thermoelectric mini fridges, wine coolers, 12V car cool boxes, some water coolers and small dehumidifiers. The module sits between two heatsinks, usually with a fan on each.

## If you lack a part
- No CPU cooler: any big aluminium heatsink with a fan, as long as the hot side stays under about 50 °C.
- No cooler box: build one from foam board in a wooden box, with a tight lid and gasket.
